newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE SEEKS PRIVATISATION ROLE.
newsitem.headline: PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE SEEKS PRIVATISATION ROLE.

text.p: Months of frustration about privatisation plans erupted in the parliamentary committee on public enterprise on Tuesday with a proposal for an independent policy-making initiative on the sale of state assets.

Members of the multi-party committee bickered with Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) chairman Mandla Msomi for almost two hours over his communication and management of the committee and over the slow progress towards a firm policy on privatisation.

ANC members Aubrey Mokoena and Ntshadi Tsheole told Msomi the committee should make its own plans to draft a "green paper" or discussion document as a first step towards policy formulation on the restructuring and privatisation of state assets.
"We must take the bull by the horns and go for a green paper of our own," said Mokoena.

IFP member Hermanthkumar Neerahoo accused government ministries of trying to "hijack" the privatisation process and take the decision-making away from Public Enterprises Miniser Stella Sigcau and the committee.
"We are completely paralysed. This committee just does not function," opposition National Party member Anna van Wyk told Reuters after the meeting.

President Nelson Mandela has declared privatisation the official policy of the ANC and the government has hammered out a National Framework Agreement (NFA) with labour and business to govern the restructuring of state assets ranging from South AfricanAirways to state-owned leisure facilities.

Minister of Telecommunications Jay Naidoo reaffirmed last month that negotiations on the partial privatisation of the state-owned telecommunications utility are well advanced and should be concluded by March next year.
The government is also about to announce the sale of six state-owned radio stations and discussions have been launched on the partial privatisation of the country's main airports.

Privatisation and relaxation of the last foreign exchange controls on residents are frequently cited by business as the keys to foreign investment and international confidence in South Afirca's post-apartheid economy.

Though the privatisation process is well advanced, the parliametnary committee was still trying on Tuesday to put in place mechanisms that would allow it to monitor and eventually sanction the privatisation process.
Msomi blamed the parliamentary secretariat and the transport, telecommunications and finance ministries for confusion over privatisation policy making.

"The Department of Finance is taking decisions all the time that impact heavily on the Minister of Public Enterprises and she only hears about it when she is confronted with it by the Deputy President," he said.
Msomi promised, however, that a "strategy" was in place to ensure that the multi-party committee vets final government privatisation proposals before they go to the cabinet.

He said a research centre and library funded by the state-owned Eskom and Transnet utilities, both candidates for privatisation, would be opened near to parliament on October 8 to help legislators study the issues and guide policy-making.
